item.title: Scott Wolf's wife says ‘my brain turned on me’ as she apologizes to family for 'profound harm' after psychosis
item.description: Kelley Wolf's 11-slide Instagram carousel reveals her diagnosis of drug-induced mania with psychosis and a direct apology to Scott Wolf and their kids.
item.content:encoded:
More than a year after Kelley Wolf was placed under an involuntary psychiatric hold following reports of erratic behavior, the former reality star is now speaking publicly about the experience and offering an apology to her husband Scott Wolf and their family.

In an Instagram carousel, Kelley said she had been diagnosed with what she called "breakthrough drug-induced mania with psychosis," which she attributed to a combination of stress, past trauma, hormonal shifts, hallucinogens and prescribed medication.

"It’s been a year since I recognized what everyone around me could see: I was not well, and I needed help," Kelley wrote. "I felt like my brain had been hijacked, and the world was moving at the speed of a freight train."

PSYCHEDELIC THERAPY MAY BE COMING TO YOUR DOCTOR'S OFFICE AS QUESTIONS SWIRL

Kelley said she had "no awareness" of her actions at the time and was "completely delusional."

"I think one of mine was that I was in the CIA and that I was running for President!" she admitted.

PEREZ HILTON UNDER INVOLUNTARY PSYCH HOLD AFTER APPARENT SELF-HARM LIVESTREAM: SOURCE

"After a year working with incredible doctors, therapists, psychologists, and healers, I have an answer," she wrote, later adding, "I won’t recount all the chaos, but what has burdened my soul is my need to say I’m so sorry."

Kelley and the "Party of Five" actor announced in June 2025 that they were ending their 21-year marriage. Days later, she was detained by police in Utah County and taken to a hospital after making comments that concerned others.

JENNIFER LOPEZ TAKES BLAME FOR BEN AFFLECK DIVORCE, SAYS SHE NEEDED TO 'FIGURE' HERSELF OUT AFTER SPLIT

In her new post, Kelley said the behavior that followed caused "profound harm" to those closest to her.

"My husband of twenty years was taken through a nightmare that wouldn’t even fly in a movie script; it was so brutal," she wrote. "The things I did, said, wrote, and posted caused profound harm and were not based in truth or reality. And they caused pain I could never imagine to the people I love the most."

"My brain turned on me," she continued. "In my illness, I made accusations and did things that make me shudder."

Her remarks come after Scott, 58, said last year that Kelley had planned to make "false allegations" against him during their divorce proceedings. He shared alleged text messages in which she appeared to say she had been advised to make claims that she did not believe were true in an effort to gain an advantage in court.

At the time, Scott said the claims were "baseless and incredibly dangerous," particularly for the couple’s three children. A July 2025 agreement granted him temporary sole physical custody, while Kelley was allowed supervised visitation.

Kelley directly addressed Scott and the couple’s three children — Jackson, 17, Miller, 13, and Lucy Marie, 12 — in her apology, writing that the pain she caused would "haunt" her.

"It was my job to protect you, honor you, and keep you safe, and I became the cause of your heartbreak," she wrote. "I am sorry."

"You never gave up on me, and you fought like hell until you landed me in safe harbor," she wrote. "I owe you my life. I will work hard to use this life to leave it better, to pay it forward, and to never give up on the power of love."

Scott showed his support by commenting five heart emojis on Kelly's post.

item.title: Ivanka Trump takes surfing lesson in Costa Rica during latest family beach vacation getaway

item.content:encoded:

item.title: Does USC's poor opening game attendance mean Lincoln Riley's on the hot seat already?
item.description: USC's sparse crowd against San Jose State sparked roasts, but attendance history shows even playoff-bound teams struggle with noon kickoffs and heat.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 college football season is officially underway, and with it returns one of the greatest sporting traditions: criticizing crowd sizes and attendance.

This season, the culprit was USC, as the Trojans opened their 2026 season at home against San Jose State. Because college football scheduling is no longer based on what makes sense given a location, local time zones, time of year, or weather, NBC picked the 12pm Pacific Time window for kickoff.

That's always a tough time for Southern California locals, because Saturday traffic in the Los Angeles area, particularly for events around downtown LA, makes getting in and out of venues an hours-long slog. Combine it with the $60 parking a mile away, a poor quality opponent, and one of the most brutal weather days of the year, with atrocious heat and humidity, and it's a recipe for reduced attendance.

USC FOOTBALL RIPPED FOR PATHETIC CROWD AT HOME OPENER: 'ABSOLUTELY EMBARRASSING'

That's exactly what happened. And the college football world rushed to do what it does best, roast other programs. The crowd at kickoff was extremely small, though, it did fill in a bit more by late in the first quarter. Unsurprisingly, with the game already decided in the first 15-18 minutes and the awful conditions, it quickly emptied out.

Many commentators rushed to say that the low turnout is why USC will not make the College Football Playoff this year, while adding that Lincoln Riley is officially on the hot seat. And to be fair to those uninformed opinions, there's little doubt that USC's underwhelming performances in recent years contributed to the poor showing. But one thing those commentators, and most fans, completely misunderstand, is that attendance and fan support has quite literally nothing to do with team quality.

This phenomenon though, continues to have widespread support across college football. Fans show up to watch Arkansas on seven days a year, therefore Arkansas must be a good program with good players. Does it matter if the Razorbacks finish 2-10? Does that make them a bad program? Apparently not, because their fans showed up to watch them lose.

Then there's the other, oft-ignored part of this discussion: fan attendance at big programs in hot weather in the heat has often been a problem. Here's how one story covering the Florida Gators' struggles to fill up their stadium for noon kickoffs described "The Swamp."

"As I enter the stadium a few minutes before kickoff, the audio system rumbles through the cement pillars and I’m ready for an overwhelming surge of energy. But when I make it out into the open air, the first thing I notice are empty metal bleachers reflecting rays of bright Florida sun. While the alumni section I’m standing in is filled, the top third of the student section opposite me is mostly empty, a scatter-plot weighted toward the bottom. I was expecting the frenzied vibe of a rave; what I’ve got is more of a buzzy mimosa brunch."

And that was a highly attended game, according to Tyler Nettuno, a reporter for the school paper explained.

"The general admission seats above both end zones are patchy, too. 'For a 12 o’clock game,' Nettuno continues, 'this is the best I’ve seen it.'"

The story goes on to point out that "Ohio State, Virginia Tech and Ole Miss suffered declines of greater than 5%" in attendance. As well as the fact that Clemson didn't sell out a single game in a year they won a National Championship. While Ohio State fans explained they'd rather go sit at a bar with friends or at home instead of watching a blowout win over Florida Atlantic.

In 2025, crowd shots of a mostly empty "Death Valley" at LSU went viral on college football Twitter.

Attendance has little to do with whether a team is headed for a playoff spot. And the reasons behind the national decline in attendance are obvious. It's easier than ever to watch games through streaming services on phones. Ticket prices continue to increase, even as everyday life becomes increasingly expensive. Staying home in bad weather allows fans to track other games instead of being in miserable heat to watch a blowout win. Many younger alumni aren't as dedicated to football either, as schools bolster their academic admission standards or push for more STEM students.

Not to mention that we ran this experiment, on how much crowds impact outcomes in home games during COVID, and found that, at least in the NFL, league average home field advantage essentially stayed almost identical from 2019-2020. Fans and fan noise just don't matter as much as they'd like to believe.

So with that established, did the Trojans 42-26 win over San Jose State tell us anything about their hopes of reaching the College Football Playoff? No, not really.

Opposing fans ready to bury USC and Riley, particularly the ever-disgruntled Oklahoma fans, jumped all over the poor fourth quarter performance. And justifiably so. But when USC's starters were in the game, they dominated.

In the first half, for example, San Jose State had five drives. On four of them, the Spartans gained a total of 36 yards. Their first quarter "offense" was six plays for 11 yards and two punts. They did have one drive go 66 yards on 14 plays before a turnover on downs. But overall, their offense averaged just 3.9 yards per play and gained 102 total yards. Their first drive of the third quarter was a three-and-out with six yards. So while the starters and second string were in the game, SJSU gained 108 yards on 29 plays.

To their credit, the Spartans were able to move the ball against the Trojans' backups and third stringers, with plenty of USC's players held out entirely due to injury concerns. But for those quick to bury them for 2026, we can look at some recent history to show that isn't warranted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

In 2024, Oregon had a 17-14 lead over Idaho midway through the fourth quarter. They needed their starters to score a final touchdown with five minutes left to win 24-14 as 45.5 point favorites. They made the playoff at the end of that season.

In 2025, the eventual SEC champion Georgia Bulldogs had a two possession lead over FCS team Austin Peay until midway through the fourth quarter, leaving their starters in before securing an unimpressive 28-6 win as 48.5 point favorites.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Also in 2025, eventual undefeated national champions Indiana beat Old Dominion 27-14 in week one and allowed 218 rushing yards and 314 total yards with nearly seven yards per play. They were 24-point favorites.

So are there reasons for concern around USC? Sure, the backups will be needed throughout the season, and the poor fourth quarter wasn't encouraging. Riley hasn't exactly given fans reasons for confidence at SC, and it's clear that their secondary needs work.

But Jayden Maiava was 25/29 for 286 yards and two touchdowns without playing a particularly impressive game, by his standards. The Trojans spread the ball around, and their impressive freshman defensive end Luke Wafle made national highlights. Nobody knows whether SC can make the leap and make the playoff, despite their difficult schedule. There is one thing for certain though, an understandably bad crowd and fourth quarter didn't tell us anything.

item.title: Americans warned against travel plans as terrorism threatens popular destination
item.description: The State Department's Level 3 advisory warns of terrorism and unrest in Israel, with some areas near Gaza carrying a Level 4 "Do Not Travel" warning.
item.content:encoded:
Americans planning travel to Israel are being urged to reconsider those plans as the U.S. State Department warns of terrorism and unrest, with some areas carrying an even higher warning due to armed conflict.

The department recently reissued Israel's Level 3 advisory, "Reconsider Travel," though officials said there was no change to the overall advisory level.

The State Department warns that the security environment in Israel is complex and can change quickly.

US WARNS TRAVELERS TO AVOID PICTURESQUE COUNTRY AS SECURITY RAPIDLY WORSENS

"Violence can occur without warning," the advisory states, adding that increased regional tensions can cause airlines to cancel or limit flights into and out of Israel.

Some areas carry the highest Level 4, "Do Not Travel," warning due to armed conflict.

Americans are advised not to travel to areas north of Route 85 to Route 90 south to Route 87, within seven miles of the Gaza Strip or within 1.5 miles of the Israel-Egypt border, except around the Taba border crossing.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

U.S. government employees working in Israel are also restricted from traveling to those areas — and additional movement restrictions could be imposed "with little to no notice," due to increased security concerns or threats, according to the advisory.

The update on Aug. 26 also included a change for family members, who may now join U.S. government employees working in Israel.

For those Americans who decide to travel to Israel, officials recommend they stay aware of their surroundings, avoid demonstrations and crowds, and follow instructions from security and emergency officials.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Travelers are also advised to know the location of the nearest bomb shelter or other hardened shelter.

They should also have a plan to leave the country in an emergency that does not depend on U.S. government assistance, according to the advisory.

Officials further recommend buying travel insurance and checking coverage for evacuation assistance, medical care and trip cancellations.

Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for further details.

The warning comes as U.S. officials continue issuing travel and security alerts for destinations around the world.

Fox News Digital previously reported that U.S. officials temporarily suspended government activities and travel to Mexicali, Mexico, last week after receiving information about a potential security threat.

Americans were urged to avoid government buildings, remain aware of their surroundings and follow instructions from Mexican law enforcement. 

The suspension has since been lifted and government activities have resumed.

Andrea Margolis of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

item.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: University of Pennsylvania professor calls for litmus test for all Democratic candidates
item.description: Michael Mann demands a court packing litmus test for all Democratic candidates, joining Kamala Harris and Pete Buttigieg in the push to reshape the court.
item.content:encoded:
University of Pennsylvania professor Michael Mann is the vice provost for Climate Science, Policy, and Action and has pushed candidates to commit to major environmental reforms. Notably, he seemed to pivot in an interview with Peter Dominick on a podcast last week, calling for all Democratic candidates to face a litmus test on committing to pack the Supreme Court: promise to pack or get the sack.

It is only the latest example of how the hostile takeover of the court is now the priority for many Democrats in removing a barrier to a radical agenda.

"When it comes to Senate races, there should be a litmus test," Mann said. "It isn’t just good enough to be a Democrat. You’ve got to be a Democrat who would be willing to expand the Supreme Court … There’s no way not to be partisan. There’s no way not to be political here. If you care about the environment, you’ve got to vote for the Democrats now."

JONATHAN TURLEY: DEM SOCIALIST RIPS ‘INSTITUTIONALISTS’ AS FAR LEFT TURNS UP HEAT ON DEFENDERS OF CONSTITUTION

Establishment candidates are offering the mob the Supreme Court to show their bona fides as the far left turns on "institutionalists" who support our constitutional system. As I previously wrote, even law professors and deans joined this movement in calling for the rejection of our Constitution on the 250th anniversary of our revolution.

Once packed, the court could greenlight a variety of unconstitutional measures.

Years ago, Harvard professor Michael Klarman laid out a radical agenda to change the system to guarantee Republicans "will never win another election." However, he warned that the Supreme Court "could strike down everything I just described." Therefore, the court must be packed in advance to make these changes possible.

That includes an agenda for extreme measures ranging from wealth taxes, to reparations, to climate control regulations.

MORNING GLORY: END THE FILIBUSTER, PACK THE COURT, KISS THE CONSTITUTION GOODBYE

Mann raised the need to reverse doctrines limiting agency authority — a barrier to some climate control measures. In so doing, he got the underlying law fundamentally wrong: "It was in a conservative Supreme Court decision within the last few years that introduced the so-called Chevron standard. Basically, what they said was that the EPA no longer had the authority to make rules based on the science and its own determination."

In 2024, the Supreme Court actually overturned the Chevron Doctrine in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. It also did not rule that "the EPA no longer had the authority to make rules based on the science and its own determination." Rather, it said that courts would review such decisions without the prior presumptions in favor of agency decision-making. The restored, traditional judicial review is precisely to determine whether agency decisions are based on credible interpretations of the law and science.

Mann has had his own conflicts with the courts. He was sanctioned last year after winning a defamation case against bloggers Rand Simberg and Mark Steyn for attacking his climate control research.

KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN

At the time, some of us questioned the award, which was just $1 in actual damages but $1 million in punitive damages. In 1996, the U.S. Supreme Court decided a case, BMW of North America v. Gore, striking down a punitive damages award. The case involved the company’s practice of repairing and repainting cars damaged in transit without telling the customers.

The jury in the original trial awarded $4,000 in compensatory damages for the car’s lost value due to the lack of a factory paint job and other damage and then imposed $4 million in punitive damages for the company’s dishonesty.

D.C. Superior Court Judge Alfred S. Irving Jr. reduced the award against Steyn to just $5,000 after finding the original award to be "grossly excessive."

The court later learned that Mann’s defense team had allegedly presented false accounts of his losses after the criticism. Mann’s legal team was accused of presenting a chart listing a grant that Mann allegedly lost due to the defamatory remarks as $9.7 million, when it was later found to be worth $112,000. Irving also found a disparity in the grant income figures given to the jury.

The court found the alleged misrepresentations to be "an affront to the Court’s authority" and sanctioned Mann and his legal team "for bad-faith trial misconduct." After reversing the jury verdict, the court ordered Mann to pay $1.1 million of his critics’ legal expenses.

Now, Mann is calling for all Democratic candidates to pledge to pack the Supreme Court as a condition for running — so any Democrat who believes in our institutions and resists this mob will be a persona non grata in the party as an "institutionalist" captured by "nostalgia."

Mann joins a growing list of figures demanding the hostile takeover of the court — from former Vice President Kamala Harris to former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. The priority is telling.

CARVILLE TELLS DEMS TO QUIETLY PREPARE POWER GRAB WITH DC, PUERTO RICO STATEHOOD AND SUPREME COURT PACKING

Much of what is planned by the far left will be difficult to accomplish due to constitutional limits. You can remove those limits by eliminating an independent Supreme Court and turning this essential institution into a federal version of state courts packed with partisan jurists.

At its base, is a fundamental misunderstanding of the court’s role. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., not only renewed her previous call to pack the court but said the court was illegitimate for rendering decisions against "widely held public opinion." However, the court was meant to be counter-majoritarian to protect minority groups and viewpoints from the majority will.

Mann’s advice is different from that of James Carville, who wants Democrats to hide this intended move from the public — which continues to oppose court packing. Carville told Democratic candidates: "If the Democrats win the presidency and both houses of Congress, I think on day one, they should expand the Supreme Court to 13. F--- it. Eat our dust. Don’t run on it. Don’t talk about it. Just do it."

Mann and others, including former Attorney General Eric Holder, are done with any pretense: "There’s no way not to be partisan. There’s no way not to be political here."

In other words, it is time to make the Supreme Court itself partisan and political. It will then be reduced to just another partisan institution in an age of rage.

item.title: Justin Rose slam dunks hole-in-one during final round of Tour Championship on extremely difficult Par 3
item.description: Justin Rose's slam-dunk hole-in-one on the Par 3 9th at the Tour Championship stole the show, moments after Scottie Scheffler nearly aced No. 2.
item.content:encoded:
Justin Rose was putting together a forgettable final round at the Tour Championship on Sunday, but then things changed in an instant with one swing on the par 3 ninth hole.

Standing on the ninth tee at 2-over par for the day and well out of contention in the PGA Tour's season finale, Rose grabbed a six-iron out of his bag and proceeded to hit the perfect shot, literally. The Par 3 was playing 208 yards on Sunday, and it isn't necessarily the ideal spot to turn around your day with the hole demanding a lengthy carry over water, but it didn't bother the Englishman.

Rose struck his iron perfectly, and seconds later, he got to witness his ball disappear into the bottom of the hole.

While every ace is rare and unique, they don't get much better than a slam-dunk hole-in-one that never touches land until it actually finds the cup.

GOLFER SMASHES CAR'S WINDSHIELD WITH TEE SHOT, GETS CONFRONTED BY CAR ON COURSE, THEN ACES VERY NEXT HOLE

Rose was sure to celebrate accordingly, like most would, by simply holding his arms up in the air before slamming his finger down to mimic what everyone had just witnessed his golf ball do.

Unfortunately for Rose, he followed up the ace on the ninth hole with a bogey on the Par 4 tenth, but what he managed to pull off on Sunday will be something he won't forget for a long, long time.

World No. 1 Scottie Scheffler almost joined in on the hole-in-one fun moments before Rose managed his ace when he hit it to inside three inches on the Par 3 second hole.

Rose, the FedEx Cup winner in 2018, picked up the 13th PGA Tour win of his career earlier this year at the Farmers Insurance Open, and did so in dominating fashion, besting the field by seven shots.

The 46-year-old will assuredly be looking to strengthen his resume during the 2027 season while looking to make the European Ryder Cup team for what will be his eighth appearance in the biennial event when it heads to Ireland next fall.

item.title: DC public schools face special grand jury probe into attendance, truancy and graduation records
item.description: A special grand jury is probing D.C. public schools over truancy, graduation rates and how attendance records are documented across campuses.
item.content:encoded:
Federal prosecutors have launched a rare special grand jury probe into D.C. public schools, zeroing in on truancy, graduation rates and attendance records.

The investigation, which was first reported by The Washington Post, is examining the supervision and oversight of young people in the nation’s capital, according to people familiar with the matter.

This is about "safeguarding youth in the District," a law enforcement official told Fox News.

Teachers and other personnel at several D.C. Public Schools campuses have been contacted in recent days about student absences, graduation practices and the way attendance is documented, the Washington Post reported. At least one person has already testified before the panel, while others are expected to appear in the coming days, according to the outlet.

DETROIT SCHOOLS OFFER STUDENTS UP TO $1,000 FOR PERFECT ATTENDANCE AS PROGRAM EXPANDS

The use of a special grand jury is unusual. Fox News is told a judge must approve the creation of such a panel, which can conduct a sweeping investigation and issue a detailed report on its findings even if prosecutors ultimately file no criminal charges.

A spokesperson for U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office told the Washington Post it could neither confirm nor deny an investigation.

The office of D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser said its focus remains on the new school year.

"Our focus remains on welcoming students and families back for a strong start to the new school year, and that is what we want our principals and teachers focused on as well," the mayor’s office told the Washington Post. "We make all school data public and will continue to do so."

CHAOTIC TEEN BRAWL GOES VIRAL AFTER TEEN TERROR PROMPTS US ATTORNEY PIRRO'S PLAN TO PROSECUTE PARENTS

The Washington Post reported that senior prosecutor Steven Vandervelden, one of Pirro’s top allies in the U.S. attorney’s office, is overseeing the inquiry.

Pirro has repeatedly linked school truancy to youth crime and disruptive teen gatherings in the District. At a May news conference, she said authorities could take action when teens repeatedly break curfew or skip school.

GRADY JUDD PUTS PARENTS ON NOTICE OVER TIKTOK TEEN TAKEOVERS: 'WE'RE GONNA COME LOCK YOU UP TOO'

"We’re coming for you, and we’re coming for your parents," Pirro said.

She also said her office wanted school records involving students accused of chronic truancy and curfew violations, according to the Washington Post. The outlet reported that the city did not voluntarily turn over those records.

EXPLOSIVE REPORT FINDS $230M IN ALLEGED K-12 EDUCATION FRAUD AMID TRUMP'S CRACKDOWN: 'ESPECIALLY HIDEOUS'

The new probe comes years after D.C. schools were rocked by a graduation scandal centered on Ballou High School. A 2018 city investigation found the school had awarded diplomas to students who failed to satisfy attendance rules or had improperly completed makeup coursework.

While the scandal initially centered on Ballou High School, it eventually spread to several D.C. high schools. The investigation found that about one-third of D.C. students who graduated in 2017 had not actually met the requirements for a diploma, according to the Washington Post. District officials later said they tightened enforcement of attendance standards.

MORE THAN 400K NEW YORK CITY CHILDREN ENROLLED IN FAILING PUBLIC SCHOOLS: REPORT

Absenteeism, however, has persisted. During the 2023-24 school year, nearly 16,000 D.C. Public Schools students, roughly one-third of K-12 enrollment, were considered truant after missing at least two weeks of classes without an excuse, the Washington Post reported last year.

The special grand jury’s work is unfolding as D.C.’s school system, which serves more than 50,000 students, begins a new academic year.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Office of the State Superintendent of Education for comment.

item.title: Trump vows to report NBC anchor Kristen Welker to FCC over 'purposeful inaccuracy' on endorsements
item.description: Trump announced on Truth Social that Kristen Welker will be reported to the FCC after she described his primary endorsement record as mixed results.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that NBC's "Meet the Press" host Kristen Welker would be reported to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for potential punishment after she characterized his primary endorsement record as producing mixed results.

"Kristen Welker, the Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has ‘mixed results’ on his Endorsements of Candidates, when the recent WINS of Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei, stand at 100% for the U.S. Senate, and 98% for the U.S. House, recently and over the longterm," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.

"How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached," Trump continued. "Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment. Unfortunately, she is not the only one."

NBC News defended Welker in a statement to Fox News Digital on Sunday, backing its "Meet the Press" moderator following Trump’s threat.

FROM ABC LICENSE REVIEWS TO COMEY INDICTMENTS, TRUMP'S REGULATORY WAR ON CRITICS ENTERS NEW PHASE

"Trump is getting more explicit about weaponizing the FCC. This morning he said @kwelkernbc will be ‘reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment’ for saying something he didn’t like about his endorsement record. (By law, the FCC can’t punish Welker.) And that’s not all..." Stelter posted to X.

A Fox News Trump Primary Endorsement Tracker published Thursday found Trump-backed candidates had won all 24 Republican Senate primaries in which he endorsed and 214 of 218 House primaries, producing a 100% Senate success rate and a roughly 98% House rate.

The two victories Trump identified came Tuesday. Graham defeated Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina’s Senate runoff, while former state Sen. Mike Mazzei defeated Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond by approximately 2,000 votes for the Republican gubernatorial nomination.

Trump accused news organizations of using his losses to discount a broader record he described as historically strong.

In actuality, it is, without question, the strongest Endorsement in the History of Politics," Trump said.

He ended his post by appealing directly to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.

FCC CHAIR SUGGESTS ABC SKIPPING TRUMP'S SPEECH WILL FACTOR IN LICENSE RENEWAL DECISION

"The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously," Trump said.

Carr has previously warned broadcasters that news distortion could affect license renewals.

The FCC, however, licenses individual stations rather than networks such as NBC, and its published policy requires evidence that a report was deliberately intended to mislead viewers, distinguishing deliberate distortion from an inaccuracy or difference of opinion.

Fox News Digital reached out to the FCC for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: California bill recognizing 2 Islamic holidays nears Newsom’s desk
item.description: Gavin Newsom could soon decide whether California public schools and state workers get formal recognition of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha holidays.
item.content:encoded:
California could soon formally recognize two of Islam’s most important holy days under legislation that would give state workers greater flexibility to take them off and allow public schools to close in observance of the holidays.

The measure, which overwhelmingly passed the state Assembly and is awaiting Senate action, would recognize Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha in state law and could soon head to Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk.

Assembly Bill 2017, introduced by Democratic San Francisco Assemblymember Matt Haney, passed the Assembly 64-1 in late May. It must clear the Senate before the legislative session ends Monday to reach Newsom.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

The bill would let state employees use existing paid holiday credits to take time off for Eid. Public schools and community colleges could also close for the holidays.

"California is home to one of the largest and most vibrant Muslim communities in the country, and their traditions deserve recognition and respect," Haney said in a news release about the bill in March. "No student should have to choose between celebrating one of the holiest days of their faith and showing up to school, and no worker should feel they have to sacrifice their religious observance."

Haney also said the bill is also about treating Muslim Californians equally.

"AB 2017 is about making sure Muslim Californians are seen, valued, and treated with the same dignity as every other community in our state," he said.

Eid al-Fitr, or the "Festival of Breaking the Fast," marks the end of Ramadan, the Islamic holy month when Muslims fast from dawn to sunset. Eid al-Adha, or the "Festival of Sacrifice," commemorates the willingness of the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham) to sacrifice his son in obedience to God.

CALIFORNIA SCHOOL DISTRICT SUED OVER FIELD TRIP TO MOSQUE WHERE STUDENTS ALLEGEDLY DONNED MUSLIM GARB

Supporters say the bill would make it easier for Muslim workers and students to take part in Eid prayers and spend the holidays with their families.

"For decades, Muslim families across the state have had to navigate an unfair balancing act between their faith and their academic or professional obligations," Oussama Mokeddem, legislative and government affairs director for the Council on American-Islamic Relations’ (CAIR) California chapter, said in a statement in July. "AB 2017 is a meaningful step toward ensuring Muslim students can celebrate Eid with the same dignity, respect, and accommodation afforded to other faith communities."

Hala Hijazi, founder of the Muslim Impact Council, recalled missing Eid with her family earlier in her career while working for the city of San Francisco.

"It was really painful to not be with my family," Hijazi told the Sacramento Bee. She said her family would go to lunch after Eid al-Fitr services and give gifts to the children.

The California Family Council, a conservative Christian advocacy group, opposes the bill’s school provisions, while saying it supports allowing students to take time off for religious holidays.

FEDERAL COURT UPHOLDS TEXAS LAW REQUIRING TEN COMMANDMENTS IN PUBLIC CLASSROOMS

The group objects to language allowing schools to hold exercises "acknowledging and celebrating the meaning and importance" of Eid. It also criticized a provision allowing the State Board of Education to develop a model curriculum guide for those exercises.

"No California statute authorizes public schools to hold exercises celebrating the meaning of Christmas, Easter, or Good Friday," the group said in a May statement, arguing Christian and Jewish holidays have not received comparable treatment. "The asymmetry is written into the law."

If signed into law, Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha would join other holidays California has recognized, including Lunar New Year and Diwali.

California would not be the first state to recognize the Eid holidays. Washington was the first, according to the Sacramento Bee. Hijazi told the newspaper that California’s proposal would go further by allowing state workers to use paid holiday credits, while Washington allows unpaid time off.

item.title: What Meta's new teen restrictions mean for young people
item.description: Meta's new teen accounts settlement sets a default two-hour daily limit on Instagram and Facebook, plus night mode and school mode restrictions.
item.content:encoded:
If you have ever asked a teenager to put down a phone and heard, "Just one more minute," you already know how hard screen limits can be to enforce.

Now Meta has agreed to a sweeping child-safety settlement that could reshape how teens use Facebook and Instagram across much of the United States.

A judge approved the agreement on Aug. 27. Under the deal, Meta will put a default two-hour daily cap on teen use of Facebook and Instagram combined. It will also restrict most app access overnight. Meanwhile, parents will get stronger control over settings teens may want to change.

The agreement goes well beyond a screen time reminder. Here's what will change, how the limits work, what Meta told CyberGuy and what parents can do now.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS

With the judge's approval, the agreement is now in effect, but the new protections will roll out over the coming months. Most of the major requirements have a six-month compliance deadline, while some features are due sooner. Here's how the biggest changes break down for teens and parents.

Meta will apply a default two-hour daily limit across Facebook and Instagram combined. Time spent scrolling on either app counts toward the total. In addition, Meta says it will count usage across multiple accounts when it detects that one teen operates more than one account.

Direct messaging, time spent in settings and qualifying long-form audio or video are excluded from the two-hour limit. Under the agreement, qualifying long-form content generally means audio or video that lasts at least 22 minutes and has not been artificially extended.

A teen can only turn off the two-hour limit with a parent's permission. That creates a much firmer stopping point than another reminder that can be dismissed.

Night Mode will block most Facebook and Instagram activity from midnight to 6 a.m. During that window, teens will no longer be able to view or post to areas such as Feed, Stories, Explore or Reels.

Direct messaging will remain available. That exception lets teens continue communicating with friends and family. For families dealing with late-night scrolling, this could create a clearer boundary without requiring someone to change the setting every evening.

Meta will also disable push notifications by default from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m., except for urgent account security or platform integrity alerts. Parents using supervision can change that setting.

School Mode focuses on daytime distractions. From 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Friday between Aug. 15 and June 15, Meta will mute most push notifications by default.

However, teens will still be able to receive direct messages. Meta will also allow account security and safety alerts during those hours. The idea is simple. A school day should come with fewer reasons to keep checking Instagram or Facebook.

Meta will also add more frequent reminders. Teens will receive a prompt after every 15 minutes of continuous screen time on Facebook or Instagram. In addition, Meta will send prompts when total daily use reaches 60 minutes and again at 90 minutes.

The settlement requires these prompts and pauses to be implemented within four months of the agreement's effective date.

Those alerts arrive before a teen reaches the two-hour limit. As a result, the hard cap becomes the final boundary rather than the first warning.

The agreement also changes parts of the viewing experience. Teens will be able to choose a non-personalized feed as their default. That feed will avoid Meta's recommendation systems when deciding what to show next.

Parents using supervision will be able to require that setting. Meta will also periodically remind teens that the option exists. Meanwhile, teens will be able to turn off autoplay. Parents will be able to require that setting too. With autoplay disabled, another piece of content will no longer begin automatically. The teen will need to tap or swipe to continue.

NEW MEXICO SEEKS MASSIVE PENALTY FROM META AFTER JURY FOUND TECH GIANT LIABLE FOR ENDANGERING CHILDREN

Meta will hide like and reaction totals by default for teen accounts. That applies to a teen's own posts as well as content posted by other people.

The company is also expanding its restrictions on appearance filters. Meta already blocks teens from using cosmetic surgery filters. Under the agreement, teens will also lose access to what Meta calls extreme makeup filters. These changes target parts of the social media experience that can keep attention focused on appearance and social feedback.

Age verification sits at the center of these protections. A teen limit only works if the platform correctly identifies the person behind the account.

Meta says it will invest in stronger technology to find accounts that may belong to children under 13. The company also plans to improve systems that identify users ages 13 to 17 who enter an adult birthday. Once Meta identifies those accounts, it can place them into experiences designed for teens.

Still, age detection remains one of the biggest tests ahead. A system that regularly mistakes teens for adults could weaken many of the protections in the agreement.

Meta also plans to expand its parental supervision tools. For example, parents will receive a notification when a teen links a secondary account. The company also plans alerts involving interactions with accounts it considers potentially suspicious.

In addition, parents will get periodic updates about their teen's usage and attempts to change protective settings. Those alerts could make it easier to catch changes without constantly checking a teen's account.

Meta began rolling out Teen Accounts in 2024. Those accounts brought automatic protections to younger Instagram users and added more control for parents. Meta later expanded its teen safety approach across more of its services.

CyberGuy previously covered Meta's expansion of Teen Accounts to Facebook and Messenger. Earlier tools leaned more heavily on reminders and configurable controls.

By comparison, the settlement creates stronger defaults. A teen who reaches the two-hour combined limit will need a parent's permission to turn it off. For a household where "five more minutes" somehow turns into another hour, that could feel very different.

Meta describes the financial package as approximately $18 billion. Participating states would receive about 70% of the allocated payment, or roughly $12.7 billion, over 10 years.

The remaining 30%, about $5.3 billion, depends on TikTok and YouTube meeting two conditions. First, both companies would need to implement a one-hour Daily Limit, Night Mode and age-assurance measures. Second, each would need to make a matching financial payment.

Half of Meta's remaining funds would be tied to YouTube's payment. The other half would depend on TikTok. Meta argues that restricting teens on one platform has limited impact if they can immediately move to another app. That helps explain why two of its biggest rivals play such a prominent role in the agreement.

The executed agreement also includes Snap in the broader industry-adoption framework. However, Meta's public explanation ties the matching financial-payment requirement specifically to TikTok and YouTube.

Meta responded to CyberGuy with additional information about the agreement, including an open letter calling on TikTok and YouTube to adopt the same framework. According to Meta, teens regularly move among many apps, so similar protections need to extend across the industry.

Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney made the same case in an on-camera statement provided to CyberGuy. He said, " Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution."

Mahoney also called on TikTok and YouTube to implement the framework right away. From a parent's point of view, Meta's argument is easy to understand. If Instagram closes after two hours while another social platform stays available, some teens may simply move their scrolling somewhere else.

That position also helps explain why TikTok and YouTube play such a prominent role in the settlement's financial structure.

Participation from Snap, TikTok and YouTube could trigger stricter Meta limits under the agreement's broader industry-adoption framework. The agreement requires most of its provisions to remain in place for 10 years. However, Meta's Time Limit and Night Mode commitments initially run for five years.

If industry peers join the agreement, those commitments extend to 10 years. The defaults would get tougher too.

Meta says the Daily Limit would drop to one hour per app. Night Mode would expand from midnight through 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. through 7 a.m.

As a result, participation from Meta's rivals could change both the length and strength of the restrictions.

Meta says social media platforms should not shoulder the entire age-verification process on their own. The company argues that app stores should provide developers with verified age information. According to Meta, that could help apps apply age-appropriate protections more consistently.

Meta also supports legislation that would require app stores to verify a user's age and obtain parental approval before a teen downloads an app. That debate could become increasingly important as more platforms introduce age-based restrictions.

The agreement also creates outside oversight. An independent auditor will test Meta's compliance and report to participating states. Those reviews will happen annually for five years.

Meta says the agreement will also establish an independent social media research foundation. The company says it will provide consented user data to the foundation for research into teen well-being. That outside review could help show whether the protections work once they reach millions of accounts.

A judge approved the settlement on Aug. 27. While the new requirements will roll out over the coming months, families can review their teen's social media settings today. Here are several places to start.

Meta's supervision tools give parents access to additional controls and account information. Once supervision is connected, parents can review available safety settings and manage certain protections. CyberGuy has steps showing you how to activate Instagram's parental supervision tools and link your teen's account. Before changing everything, talk with your teen about the settings you plan to use. Explain what you want to protect and why.

Open the phone's screen-time dashboard and look at the numbers together. You may discover that Instagram or Facebook takes up less time than expected. Another app could be responsible for a much larger share of the day. Then, use those numbers to set limits that reflect how the phone is actually being used. CyberGuy has a deeper guide to phone safety tools for parents, including screen-time controls.

Look at who can follow, message or tag your teen. Meta says it will continue using private defaults for teen Instagram accounts. Facebook will also keep restrictive default settings for teens. Meanwhile, the company plans to make it harder for potentially suspicious adults to find or interact with younger users. Also review followers your teen no longer recognizes.

Meta says teens will remain in age-appropriate content settings by default. The company also plans to continue restricting interactions with accounts it considers inappropriate for younger users. Parents using supervision should check those controls periodically.

Facebook and Instagram make up only part of a teen's digital day. Apple Screen Time and Google Family Link can add device-level limits. Those controls become especially useful when a teen moves from one social app to another. As a result, parents can create boundaries that extend beyond Meta's platforms.

Meta's Night Mode will add an overnight barrier inside Facebook and Instagram. Families can add another layer by charging phones outside bedrooms or keeping them in a shared space overnight. A simple routine can also reduce the nightly debate over when the phone goes away.

The two-hour cap will probably grab the most attention because it creates a clear stopping point. However, the bigger change may be how many of these protections will start turned on by default.

For teens, that could mean more interruptions during long scrolling sessions, fewer overnight opportunities to browse feeds and less pressure from notifications during school hours.

Parents will also gain more visibility when a teen tries to change certain settings. Meanwhile, Meta will face independent compliance reviews during part of the agreement period.

Age detection remains a key challenge. If a 15-year-old can easily convince the system that an account belongs to an adult, many of these protections become much easier to avoid. For that reason, the rollout will tell us far more than the announcement alone.

I have watched social media companies add parental controls for years. One recurring problem keeps coming up: Parents have to find the controls before those tools can help. This agreement puts more protections on by default. A two-hour limit that requires parental permission to disable feels very different from another screen-time reminder. The overnight block could also give families some backup when late-night scrolling becomes a constant battle. I understand Meta's argument about TikTok and YouTube too. If one app closes the door while other major platforms remain available, a teen may simply move on to the next feed. Still, the real test comes as these protections roll out over the coming months. I want to see how accurately Meta identifies teen accounts and how difficult these limits are to bypass. Parents should view these tools as backup, not autopilot. Settings can create useful boundaries, but conversations at home still have to carry much of the load.

Would you want every major social media app to automatically lock teens out after a set amount of time, or should families decide those limits themselves? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

item.title: Chicago mayor demands companies reveal whether leaders ‘reflect diversity’ for city contracts
item.description: DHS accused Brandon Johnson of punishing businesses that help ICE enforce federal immigration law after the Chicago mayor signed a new executive order.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order on Wednesday requiring city contractors to disclose information about leadership diversity demographics, as well as report whether they have any ties to certain law enforcement agencies such as ICE, as he moves to use the city's purchasing power to impose new contracting standards.

Johnson said workplace data was necessary to identify discrimination and criticized the Trump administration's efforts to end federal reporting requirements.

"If you want to do business with this city, we want to know whether the people leading your company reflect the diversity of the communities whose tax dollars are paying your contracts," Johnson said.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) accused Johnson of punishing American companies for assisting federal immigration enforcement.

DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED'

"If Mayor Johnson wants to lecture anyone about taxpayer dollars, remember what he is: a sanctuary politician who bullies American companies with money that isn’t his. Chicago takes the federal check, but it won’t enforce the federal law," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Sunday.

"In case Chicago’s mayor forgot, an oath of office is a commitment to upholding the law, not encouraging criminal illegal aliens to break it," they added.

"Make no mistake, we will not be deterred. Under President Trump, ICE will keep enforcing the law in Chicago, whether City Hall likes it or not," the spokesperson said.

The Chicago mayor unveiled the order during a press conference at Arise Chicago, a nonprofit that works to protect immigrants' rights. Johnson framed the order as a response to corporate influence in Washington and said Chicago would use city spending to put its values into practice.

The order also directs Chicago's chief procurement officer to develop rules within 90 days barring vendors found to have committed public integrity, workplace discrimination or wage theft violations during the previous five years.

Contractors must disclose whether they received more than $500,000 from government or law enforcement agencies or face proceedings alleging excessive force, unlawful detention, unconstitutional policing, discrimination or other civil rights violations.

TRUMP ADMIN WANTS TO STOP ILLINOIS CITY'S REPARATIONS EFFORT FOR 'SIMPLY HANDING OUT MONEY BASED ON RACE'

Large private companies with corporate families reporting at least $1 billion in net income must provide information about leadership diversity, board composition and diversity policies when not already covered by Illinois reporting law.

Under the order, contractors must also report efforts to hire and promote formerly incarcerated people, and future awardees must update the disclosures at least annually.

Doing business with ICE alone is not listed as a disqualifying offense. The order also disqualifies firms for specified integrity, discrimination or wage theft violations while making the disclosures public.

Not With Our Money, the campaign that joined Johnson at the announcement, identified $3.19 billion in Chicago contractors held by 42 firms that also do business with ICE, according to the group's research.

DHS ISSUES SCATHING REBUKE AFTER FORMER ATLANTA MAYOR KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS TOUTS CUTTING TIES WITH ICE

Johnson was referring to an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission proposal to rescind requirements for employers and other covered entities to file annual EEO reports containing aggregate employee race, sex and job-category data. EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas said the reports risked hindering enforcement of equal employment laws and raised constitutional concerns.

The order marks Johnson’s latest clash with federal immigration authorities.

In October, Johnson barred ICE from using city parking lots and garages for operations, a policy a federal agent said forced agents to stage in public and created operational risks. DHS said Operation Midway Blitz had resulted in more than 4,500 arrests by December.

Fox News Digital reached out to Johnson's office for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Four foods you should never store in the freezer and where to keep them instead
item.description: Chef Dennis Littley of New Jersey reveals why cheese, cooked pasta, cured meats and wine may lose texture and flavor when stored in the freezer after thawing.
item.content:encoded:
The freezer can help food last longer, but some kitchen staples may be better off stored elsewhere.

Some foods can lose their texture, flavor or overall quality after being frozen and thawed, according to a recent list from food and cooking publication Food & Wine.

New Jersey-based Chef Dennis Littley, a culinary educator and founder of Ask Chef Dennis, told Fox News Digital that freezing can change a food's texture because the water inside turns into ice crystals.

PUMPKIN SPICE INVADES SUMMER AS AMERICANS KICKSTART FALL TRADITIONS EARLIER THAN EVER

"The biggest thing I tell home cooks is that being able to freeze something doesn't necessarily mean you should," Littley said.

Here are four foods that may be better stored somewhere other than the freezer.

While most cheeses can technically be frozen, Littley said doing so can leave them crumbly or grainy once thawed.

The change can be particularly noticeable with softer and creamier cheeses.

SCIENTISTS SAY YOU'VE BEEN THROWING AWAY PERFECTLY GOOD MEAT BECAUSE OF ONE COMMON MISTAKE

Instead, Littley recommends keeping cheese well wrapped in the refrigerator and buying only as much as you expect to use while it is still fresh.

Whether cooked pasta belongs in the freezer can depend on the dish.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Pasta can soften as it freezes and thaws, and creamy sauces can separate," Littley said.

For pasta dishes with creamy sauces, he recommends refrigerating leftovers and eating them within a few days rather than freezing them.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Heartier baked pasta dishes, however, can hold up better in the freezer, according to Littley.

Prosciutto, salami and other cured meats can generally be frozen, but Littley said the bigger concern is what happens to their texture and flavor afterward.

That can be especially noticeable when the meat is served on a sandwich, charcuterie board or as an appetizer, where texture can be an important part of the experience.

Littley recommends keeping cured meats wrapped in the refrigerator and using them within the recommended time after opening.

Wine is one item that Littley advises keeping out of the freezer.

"No go," he said. "The liquid expands as it freezes, which can cause problems with the bottle or cork, and you're not doing the wine's flavor and aroma any favors."

Instead, opened wine should be resealed and stored in the refrigerator, including red wine.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Red wine can then be brought back to the appropriate serving temperature before drinking, he said.

While the freezer may seem like an easy way to extend the life of many foods and drinks, Littley said proper storage can help preserve their texture, flavor and overall quality.

"Some dishes freeze beautifully, while others aren't going to come back the way you want them to," he said.

item.title: Trump surprises NASA officials with call after Roman Space Telescope launch
item.description: Trump dialed into a NASA press conference after the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy from Florida.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump unexpectedly dialed into a NASA press conference Sunday, congratulating the agency after the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope successfully launched on a nearly 1 million-mile journey into space.

Trump’s call came shortly after the telescope launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. 

NASA officials said the telescope successfully separated from the rocket and began sending telemetry as it headed toward its destination in space.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman unexpectedly walked out of the press conference holding his cell phone, saying, "The president is excited about Roman."

He returned moments later with Trump on speakerphone. The president thanked and congratulated the team.

"I just called Jared to find out, is there anything negative that I should know about, like, it will never be able to return? Little things like that," the president joked.

TRUMP TO TRANSFORM SPACEFLIGHT FROM SPECTACLE TO STATUS QUO TARGETING 3 LAUNCHES PER DAY

"He said, 'No, it's looking great. It couldn't be better. And it was another great successful launch.' Jared is doing a fantastic job. You are doing a fantastic job, and I'm supplying you [with] all that money!"

Trump then reflected on the state of NASA facilities when he first took office, praising the progress the agency has made in the intervening years.

"And now again, like we are with the country itself, we're the hottest there is. We're the hottest in space, we have the hottest country anywhere in the world. So let's keep it all going. You're a big part of it. Let's keep it all going."

NASA ANNOUNCES THREE NEW MOON MISSIONS AS AGENCY RACES TO BUILD PERMANENT LUNAR BASE BY END OF 2026

The press conference followed the successful launch of the Roman Space Telescope, which Isaacman predicted would become a household name like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope.

"Over the course of the next several months, Roman will travel nearly 1 million miles away from Earth to Lagrange point L2 and begin transmitting imagery and data back home that will contribute to world-changing science," Isaacman said.

item.title: Tuskegee University president defends dress code amid criticism: ‘Raise the bar, students will reach it’
item.description: Tuskegee University President Mark Brown says the dress code banning durags and bonnets is about workplace readiness, not respectability politics.
item.content:encoded:
Tuskegee University President Dr. Mark Brown, a retired Air Force major general, is defending the historically Black university’s renewed emphasis on student dress and conduct standards, saying the policy is aimed at preparing students for the workplace rather than policing personal style.

"If you raise the bar, students will reach it," Brown told Fox News Digital in an interview.

"Why don't we raise the bar? That's what I think we ought to do. We're unapologetic about that part."

After issuing a pre-campus arrival memo requiring a business suit and shoes for business-like meetings and professional dress in the classrooms, as well as barring non-religious head coverings, Brown said he saw that evidence of success during the first days of the school year.

SOUTHERN UNIVERSITY REQUIRES BUSINESS SUITS, BANS DU-RAGS AND OTHER HEADWEAR IN NEW DRESS CODE

"I had a wonderful time riding around and walking around the campus on the first and the second day of class," he said. "The bar was raised and it was being reached. "But the same is true as if you lower the bar, or if you go past the mistake and fail to address it: That becomes the standard. And so, you know, we are a university of standards. I believe all of higher education should be a university standards."

The university’s policy has drawn criticism from freedom of expression advocates over restrictions that include bans on items such as durags and bonnets, with some critics framing the rules as "respectability politics."

Brown, however, said the dress code should be viewed as one part of a much broader push toward student success that includes punctuality, attendance, internships, professional certifications, interview preparation and workplace readiness.

CAMPUS GRADUATION CHAOS SHOWS HIGHER EDUCATION NEEDS A SERIOUS MORAL RESET

"The focus is how do I make you a professional in whatever space you want to go in?" he said.

"Any higher education institution in the country that's not focused on student success, no matter what type of university that is, is not focused where they should be. That's why we exist. That's exactly why we exist."

The policy itself is not new, Brown said, but Tuskegee is placing "greater emphasis" on it as part of an effort to ensure graduates leave campus prepared not only with a degree, but with the habits employers expect.

"It’s not the world we wish you were going into, it’s the world you’re going to go into," Brown said. "It’s not the way that we wish an employer would perceive you. It’s the way the employer will perceive you."

CHRISTIAN UNIVERSITY AIMS TO PRODUCE 'IRREPLACEABLE' GRADUATES AS AI RESHAPES HIGHER EDUCATION

Brown said the debate over whether college is worth the cost has put greater pressure on universities to demonstrate that students are being prepared for what comes after graduation.

"What do you want when you send your son or daughter to college?" Brown said. "What do you expect us to do and what do you expect to happen four or five years from now when they graduate?"

Brown said Tuskegee wants students to leave with more than a grade-point average and a diploma.

"We want them job-ready," he said.

He pointed to punctuality as one example of a habit that may appear minor in the classroom but can carry significant consequences in the workplace.

FOX NEWS POLL: FAITH IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE US IS COLLAPSING

"Would it be sad for us to allow a student to come to class late, practice that for four to five years, and then find out that no matter how great they were with their 4.0 or 3.8 GPA, it won’t keep them that job?" he said.

Critics have also questioned whether professional dress requirements could place an added financial burden on students. Brown said Tuskegee is prepared to address that concern directly.

About 70% of students on campus are Pell Grant eligible, he said, and the university’s Golden Tigers Community Closet is available to students who need help obtaining professional clothing.

"If a student needs help with that, we’re going to help them," Brown said. "That’s not going to be the barrier between compliance and getting ready. We’re going to remove that barrier."

ELITE COLLEGES ARE LOSING AMERICA’S TRUST. COMMUNITY COLLEGES CAN WIN IT BACK

The university also plans to bring in a professional several times during the school year to teach students the details of business attire, including how to button a coat and properly wear a tie.

"I really want us to bear down and double click, to use a common term these days, on the fact that we have to care as much about what happens in school as what happens after school," he said.

Brown pointed to the school’s recent employment numbers as evidence that its approach is producing results. He said roughly 70% of students who graduated in May already had jobs lined up.

"Seven out of every 10," Brown said. "That is the challenge. That’s what we should be debating."

Brown is facing criticism from those objecting to Tuskegee's renewed emphasis on its dress code, including the Foundation for Individual Rights in Education (FIRE), a student rights advocacy group, due to restrictions on durags and other clothing associated with Black culture.

COLLEGE STUDENTS EXPRESS STRONG TRUST IN SCHOOL LEADERS DESPITE BROADER PUBLIC CYNICISM: GALLUP

"Tuskegee can’t promise students broad freedom of expression while enforcing a sweeping dress code that regulates ordinary, non-disruptive expression," FIRE Senior Program Counsel Haley Gluhanich told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Preparing students for professional life is a legitimate goal, but it does not hinge on requirements about what adults wear to class or lunch."

"As a private university, Tuskegee may choose to place other values ahead of expressive freedom, but if it does, it should be honest with current and prospective students about the limits of its commitment to free expression," Gluhanich added.

In response to criticism, Brown pointed to Tuskegee’s history, including the Tuskegee Airmen, as an example of preparing students to demonstrate competence even in a society where prejudice exists.

"My race and my ethnicity would have absolutely nothing to do about it," Brown said. "That’s not the subject. The subject is social and economic mobility and student success."

"It’s not that there wasn’t prejudice in the world," Brown said. "There’s prejudice in the world today. There’s going to be prejudice tomorrow."

CLASSICAL EDUCATION AND AI COULD RESHAPE HOW AMERICA PREPARES ITS CHILDREN

He is not dismissing broader debates over culture, expression or discrimination, but he argued that Tuskegee’s immediate responsibility is preparing its students to succeed amid those realities.

"I’m not discarding the debates," he said. "The debates are great. I think America is great because we have debate. But that’s not the purpose of the university in this sense. The purpose of a university is, while the debates go on, to be prepared."

Brown has heard the criticism but has not encountered significant pushback from Tuskegee students. He also said he has received significant positive feedback from leaders at other universities.

"This is not unique," Brown said. "If you go to many universities, they have dress codes, they have these kinds of things. Perhaps we are, at this moment, [placing] a greater emphasis."

For Brown, the larger question is whether universities view their responsibility to students as ending at graduation.

"If we think the degree ends the relationship, I do not," Brown said. "I think the relationship and the value of the time here ends down the road, when that student is getting a return on investment.

"That matters the most for those students who are economically at a disadvantage, who are using education as a springboard to do better," he concluded. "Again, every college president, chancellor – I’ve got to believe – wants that for their students.

"But do we expect them to practice that when they start work? Or isn’t the classroom an extension of that? Isn’t it a laboratory by which you practice these very important skills? I think it is."

item.title: At least 3 dead, 23 wounded in separate mass shootings less than 15 minutes apart
item.description: Police in two U.S. cities are searching for answers after separate shootings left 26 people shot overnight, including three who were killed.
item.content:encoded:
Gunfire tore through two communities in Trenton, New Jersey, and Chicago less than 15 minutes apart overnight, leaving three people dead and 23 others wounded in two mass shootings as police in both cities search for answers.

Trenton police responded to a neighborhood near 194 Locust Street at about 12:25 a.m. local time Sunday after multiple shots were reported, Trenton Mayor W. Reed Gusciora said in a statement.

First responders found 11 people who had been shot.

GUNFIRE SHATTERS TORONTO LATIN STREET FESTIVAL, LEAVING AT LEAST 2 DEAD AND MULTIPLE WOUNDED

Two were pronounced dead, while nine others were taken to Capital Health Regional Medical Center. Police have not released their conditions.

The names of those killed have not been confirmed.

Gusciora said officials were still learning about the victims but shared details about one of the people killed, a man who had been trying to turn his life around after leaving prison.

"We understand that one of the individuals who lost his life had been working to turn his life around after returning home from incarceration and had recently been recognized for his commitment to reentry and positive change," Gusciora said.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said she had been briefed on the shooting.

"As local law enforcement continues to investigate, my Attorney General remains in close contact with officials on the ground," Sherrill wrote in a post on X Sunday. "I’m thinking of the families who lost loved ones, those who were injured, and the Trenton community."

No arrests have been announced, and police have not said what may have led to the Trenton shooting.

CHICAGO OFFICERS WOUNDED IN TRAFFIC STOP SHOOTOUT AS HOLIDAY WEEKEND LEAVES 3 DEAD, 16 INJURED

Officials said 12 minutes earlier and hundreds of miles away, police in Chicago were called to another mass shooting.

Chicago police said officers were breaking up a large gathering on Chicago’s South Side at about 11:37 p.m. local time Saturday night when gunmen opened fire into a crowd, hitting 14 people.

A 35-year-old man was shot multiple times and taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he died.

Police said 14 other people — six men and seven women ranging in age from 21 to 47 — were wounded.

Several were listed in good condition, including a 26-year-old woman who was shot multiple times in the chest. The conditions of some of the other victims were not immediately known.

Police have not said what the gathering was for or what may have led to the shooting. Investigators also have not released a description of the gunmen.

Cook County Crime Stoppers is offering a reward of up to $10,000 for information leading to an arrest.

"This senseless act of violence has devastated another Chicago community and left families dealing with unimaginable pain," Executive Director Paul Rutherford said.

Beyond music, Parton built a business empire in her home state of Tennessee, with Dollywood becoming one of the state’s most popular attractions. Her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library also left a lasting impact.

Inspired by Parton’s father, who never learned to read or write, the Imagination Library sends free books to children from birth until kindergarten and has grown into an international literacy initiative that has distributed millions of books to families around the world.

Parton wanted to be buried in a bed of soft cotton after spending a lifetime draped in rhinestones, according to a tribute from her nephew posted to Instagram on the day of her death.
